blocks.text: A 32-year-old man has had a dry cough and increasing breathlessness on climbing stairs for three weeks, with white patches of thrush in his mouth. His oxygen saturation falls further when he walks around the clinic. There is no history of inherited disease, and until now he has been well. Acquired immune failure, far more common than the inherited kind, can be recognised by the infections it permits.

blocks.markdown: **Secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency** is impaired immunity resulting from another condition, treatment or exposure, rather than from an inherited defect of the immune system. It is much more common than primary immunodeficiency, and is often reversible if the cause is removed. Worldwide, the most frequent causes are **malnutrition** and **HIV infection**; in high-income settings, **drugs** and **malignancy** are leading causes.

rows: HIV (CD4⁺ T cells); measles (transient immune suppression)
Impaired lymphocyte development, thymic atrophy, reduced barriers, reduced complement and phagocyte function
Protein-energy malnutrition; micronutrient deficiency (zinc, vitamin A, iron)
Corticosteroids, chemotherapy, immunosuppressants, rituximab and other biologics, radiotherapy
Splenectomy or functional asplenia (encapsulated bacteria); nephrotic syndrome and protein-losing enteropathy (loss of IgG); burns
Diabetes mellitus (neutrophil dysfunction), chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis, alcohol excess, old age
blocks.caption: Common causes of secondary immunodeficiency

blocks.title: Always look for a cause
blocks.text: In an adult with recurrent or unusual infection, ask about drugs, nutrition, diabetes, protein loss, splenectomy and HIV risk before concluding that an inherited defect is present. Removing or treating the cause can restore immunity.

blocks.markdown: **HIV and CD4 count.** The human immunodeficiency virus infects cells carrying **CD4** (T helper cells, macrophages, dendritic cells) through the CD4 receptor and a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4). It integrates into host DNA and causes progressive loss of **CD4⁺ T cells** through direct killing and chronic immune activation, so that cell-mediated immunity fails. The **CD4 count** (cells/µL) is the principal marker of immune status, and **plasma viral load** (HIV RNA copies/mL) measures viral replication. Typical healthy adult CD4 counts are in the range of several hundred to over a thousand cells/µL (ranges vary by laboratory). Antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus and allows CD4 counts to recover.

rows: Few opportunistic infections; risks similar to the general population; TB can occur at any count
Herpes zoster, oral thrush, tuberculosis, bacterial pneumonia, seborrhoeic dermatitis
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, oesophageal candidiasis, disseminated TB; prophylaxis against Pneumocystis is recommended
Cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, cryptosporidiosis, Kaposi sarcoma and CNS lymphoma more frequent
Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex, cytomegalovirus retinitis
blocks.caption: CD4 count and risk of opportunistic infection

blocks.title: Calculating the CD4 count
blocks.prompt: A patient's full blood count shows a white cell count of 5.0 × 10^9/L with 24% lymphocytes. Flow cytometry shows that 30% of lymphocytes are CD4⁺. Calculate the absolute CD4 count in cells/µL and say which opportunistic infection requires prophylaxis at this level.

steps.text: Calculate the CD4 count per litre.
Convert litres to microlitres (1 L = 10^6 µL).

Interpret: 360 cells/µL is in the 200 to 500 band, so there is moderate deficiency with increased risk of zoster, thrush and tuberculosis, but it is above the usual 200 threshold for Pneumocystis prophylaxis.

blocks.answer: 360 cells/µL; above the Pneumocystis prophylaxis threshold, but at risk of zoster and TB.

blocks.markdown: **Opportunistic infections** are infections that cause disease mainly when the immune system is impaired. In **profound T cell deficiency** (as in advanced HIV, or after intensive immunosuppression) the characteristic organisms are those normally controlled by CD4⁺ T cells and macrophages: ***Pneumocystis jirovecii*** (pneumonia with dry cough, exertional breathlessness, hypoxia and bilateral ground-glass shadowing), ***Candida*** (oral and oesophageal), ***Cryptococcus neoformans*** (meningitis), ***Toxoplasma gondii*** (cerebral abscesses), **cytomegalovirus** (retinitis, colitis), **Mycobacterium avium complex** and *M. tuberculosis*, **JC virus** (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy), and cryptosporidium (chronic diarrhoea). Tumours linked to viruses are also more common: Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8) and EBV-related lymphomas.

blocks.caption: Viral load changes in HIV are reported on a log10 scale

blocks.title: Reading a treatment response
blocks.prompt: (Illustrative.) A patient's HIV viral load is 400,000 copies/mL before antiretroviral therapy and 400 copies/mL after 12 weeks. What is the log10 reduction, and why is it more informative than the percentage fall?

steps.text: Interpret: a 3-log fall is a 99.9% reduction. A percentage fall near 100% compresses large differences (99.9% and 99.99% look the same), whereas log differences show orders of magnitude clearly, which matters when viral load is falling towards undetectable levels.

blocks.title: Immune reconstitution
blocks.text: When antiretroviral therapy restores immunity in a patient with an untreated opportunistic infection, the recovering immune system can produce a paradoxical inflammatory worsening called immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). It is a reason for caution and specialist care in advanced disease.

points: Secondary immunodeficiency has acquired causes: HIV, malnutrition, drugs (steroids, chemotherapy, biologics), malignancy, splenectomy, protein loss, diabetes, chronic disease and ageing.
In HIV, the CD4 count stages risk: Pneumocystis prophylaxis below 200 cells/µL, toxoplasmosis and cryptococcus below about 100, MAC and CMV retinitis below about 50.
Profound T cell deficiency permits Pneumocystis, Candida, cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis, CMV and atypical mycobacteria.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a recognised cause of secondary immunodeficiency?

distractorRationale.a: BTK mutation causes a primary immunodeficiency (XLA).
distractorRationale.b: Correct: corticosteroids suppress lymphocyte and phagocyte function.
distractorRationale.c: IL2RG mutation causes primary X-linked SCID.
distractorRationale.d: C5 deficiency is a primary complement defect.

questions.explanation: Corticosteroids, chemotherapy and biologic drugs are common acquired causes of immunodeficiency. The others are inherited (primary) defects.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old in a famine region has recurrent severe infections, wasting and a very low lymphocyte count. Which cause is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: malnutrition impairs T cell development and other defences.
distractorRationale.b: XLA affects boys with antibody deficiency, without wasting due to famine.
distractorRationale.c: CGD causes abscesses and not wasting or lymphopenia.
distractorRationale.d: Selective IgA deficiency is generally mild.

questions.explanation: Malnutrition is the commonest cause of immunodeficiency worldwide, causing thymic atrophy and lymphopenia with impaired barrier and cell-mediated immunity.

questions.stem: A man with nephrotic syndrome develops recurrent pneumococcal infections and has low serum IgG. Which mechanism explains this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: heavy proteinuria causes loss of small proteins, including IgG.
distractorRationale.c: BTK deficiency is inherited and X-linked.
distractorRationale.d: Excess complement does not explain low IgG.

questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy urinary protein loss including IgG, producing secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia and susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria.

questions.stem: A patient with HIV has a CD4 count of 150 cells/µL. Which action is most appropriate based on this count?

options.text: Start prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia as indicated by local guidelines

questions.correctOptionText: Start prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia as indicated by local guidelines

distractorRationale.a: Correct: below about 200 cells/µL, Pneumocystis prophylaxis is generally advised.
distractorRationale.b: Risk is clearly raised at this count.
distractorRationale.c: Live vaccines may be hazardous at low counts.
distractorRationale.d: The cause is already known to be HIV.

questions.explanation: A CD4 count under about 200 cells/µL is the usual threshold for Pneumocystis prophylaxis. Exact thresholds follow local guidelines.

questions.stem: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 40 cells/µL has headache, fever and neck stiffness for ten days. India ink staining of cerebrospinal fluid shows encapsulated yeast. Which organism is the likely cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: encapsulated yeast on India ink indicates cryptococcal meningitis.
distractorRationale.b: Pneumococcus would be seen as Gram-positive diplococci.
distractorRationale.c: Neisseria would be seen as Gram-negative diplococci.

questions.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast and a major cause of meningitis in profound T cell deficiency (CD4 below about 100). India ink highlights its capsule.

questions.stem: True or false: cerebral toxoplasmosis is characteristically seen in HIV infection when the CD4 count has fallen below about 100 cells/µL.
questions.explanation: Reactivation of latent Toxoplasma gondii causing ring-enhancing brain lesions occurs mainly in profound T cell deficiency, typically with CD4 counts below about 100 cells/µL (thresholds vary by guideline). It reflects loss of CD4⁺ T cell and macrophage control.

questions.stem: A patient has a total white cell count of 4.0 × 10^9/L, of which 25% are lymphocytes, and 20% of the lymphocytes are CD4⁺. Calculate the absolute CD4 count in cells/µL.
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes = 4.0 × 10^9 × 0.25 = 1.0 × 10^9/L. CD4⁺ cells = 1.0 × 10^9 × 0.20 = 2.0 × 10^8/L = 200 cells/µL, since 1 L contains 10^6 µL.

questions.stem: Before treatment an HIV viral load is 250,000 copies/mL. After therapy it is 250 copies/mL. Calculate the log10 reduction.
questions.explanation: The ratio is 250,000/250 = 1000, and log10(1000) = 3. A 3-log reduction corresponds to a 99.9% fall in viral load.

questions.stem: List five causes of secondary immunodeficiency and for each give the mechanism by which immunity is impaired.
markingGuide: HIV: depletion of CD4⁺ T cells
Corticosteroids/chemotherapy/biologics: suppress or kill immune cells
Malnutrition: impaired lymphocyte development, barrier and phagocyte function
Haematological malignancy: marrow replacement, defective antibody production
Splenectomy, nephrotic syndrome (IgG loss), diabetes (neutrophil dysfunction), chronic disease or ageing
questions.explanation: Secondary immunodeficiency reflects acquired loss, suppression or dysfunction of immune components.

questions.stem: Explain how the CD4 count is used to stage the risk of opportunistic infection in HIV and give examples of infections characteristic of profound T cell deficiency.
markingGuide: CD4 count falls as HIV progresses; viral load measures replication
Above 500: low risk; 200 to 500: zoster, thrush, TB, bacterial pneumonia
Below 100: toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis; below 50: MAC, CMV retinitis
Characteristic organisms are controlled by T cells and macrophages; thresholds vary by guideline
questions.explanation: The lower the CD4 count, the broader the range of opportunistic organisms that can cause disease.
